en.title: Buying food
en.summary: How to ask for food and quantities in a shop, and how to talk about prices per kilo.

paragraphs: Buying food requires words for quantities and containers, and a clear way of asking the price. In this lesson you will practise them in a typical shop conversation.
Mrs Hall is buying fruit and vegetables at a greengrocer's in Leeds.

lines.speaker: Assistant
lines.text: Good morning. Can I help you?

lines.speaker: Mrs Hall
lines.text: Yes, I would like a kilo of apples and half a kilo of tomatoes, please.

lines.speaker: Assistant
lines.text: Of course. Do you want the red apples or the green ones?

lines.speaker: Mrs Hall
lines.text: The red ones, please. How much are they?

lines.speaker: Assistant
lines.text: They are two pounds ninety a kilo. Anything else?

lines.speaker: Mrs Hall
lines.text: A bunch of bananas, and a small cucumber.

lines.speaker: Assistant
lines.text: That is eight pounds fifty altogether. Would you like a bag?

lines.speaker: Mrs Hall
lines.text: No, thank you. I have my own.

paragraphs: **1. Uncountable foods need a unit.** You cannot say two milks in a shop; say a litre of milk. The unit is countable, the food is not. See Introduction to Grammar: Substantives (nouns).

blocks.html:
UnitExample
a kilo ofa kilo of apples
a litre ofa litre of milk
a loaf ofa loaf of bread
a packet ofa packet of rice
a bunch ofa bunch of bananas

paragraphs: **2. How much for uncountable nouns and prices; how many for countable nouns.** How much is it? asks the price. See Introduction to Grammar: Questions and negation.

blocks.html:
QuestionUsed for
How much is this?price of one thing
How much are they?price of several things
How much milk do you want?uncountable amount
How many apples do you want?countable number

items: Anything else? is the usual question at the end.
A greengrocer sells fruit and vegetables; a butcher sells meat; a baker sells bread.
Some British shops charge for plastic bags, so people bring their own.

paragraphs: Most people in Britain buy food at supermarkets, but weekly markets and local shops are still popular, especially for fresh fruit and vegetables. Prices in shops show the cost per kilo, so compare them before buying.
